title: Why do we get goosebumps? 🥶
description:
Goosebumps are a tiny muscle at work: the arrector pili. Cold (or a strong feeling) fires a nerve, the muscle squeezes, the hair stands up and the skin bunches into a bump. On furry animals that traps warm air and makes them look bigger; we lost the fur but kept the reflex.

Sources: https://www.health.harvard.edu/blog/wondering-about-goosebumps-of-course-you-are-2020080320688 ; https://livescience.com/32349-what-causes-goose-bumps.html ; https://neurosciencenews.com/goosebumps-reason-16669/

scenes.say: Why does cold make your skin look like a plucked *goose*?
Blame a tiny muscle. Almost every hair on your body has its *own*.
Here's your skin, cut open. That red one is the *arrector pili*.
Relaxed, your hair lies flat. Get cold, a nerve fires, and the muscle *squeezes*.

scenes.say: The hair stands up, and the skin bunches into a bump. A *goosebump*.

scenes.say: Now times that by *thousands* of hairs.
Why bother? On a furry animal, fluffed-up fur traps a blanket of *warm air*.
